name: Engine adjustment factors
summary: Multipliers the engine applies to a type's baseline hard cost: quality tier, project size (economies of scale), IBC construction type, height above the typical story count, and prevailing-wage/union labor. Quality tiers come from the low/high spreads in RLB's Q3 2026 cost table (18 US cities); construction-type factors from the ICC Building Valuation Data (Aug 2025) and the Terner Center's California regression; prevailing wage from Terner Center studies. Size and height factors are derived and should be verified. Apply construction-type factors as a ratio: factor(selected) / factor(type's typical construction type).

items.name: Quality tier — economy

range.method: RLB Q3 2026 per-city LOW / (LOW+HIGH)/2, median across 18 US cities by building type: office secondary 0.83, office prime 0.75, retail center 0.74, hotel 3-star 0.81, warehouse 0.77, multifamily 0.75, single-family 0.67, high school 0.79, university 0.83 (e1-e3). Mid 0.79 = median of these ratios; low/high bracket them.

items.notes: The RLB low end of a city range reflects simpler specification as well as easier sites, so this slightly overstates pure finish-quality savings.

range.method: Definition: the type files' baseline hard cost is the standard-quality price.

RLB Q3 2026 per-city HIGH / (LOW+HIGH)/2, median across 18 US cities: office secondary 1.17, office prime 1.25, retail center 1.26, hotel 5-star 1.20, hotel 3-star 1.19, warehouse 1.23, multifamily 1.25, single-family 1.33, university 1.17 (e1-e3). Mid 1.21 = median.

items.name: Quality tier — luxury

range.method: Class-to-class step-ups in the same cities: RLB hotel 5-star vs 3-star midpoint ratio median 1.46 (e2); office prime vs secondary 1.65 (e1). HVS median cost per room: full-service $467k vs select-service ~$200k (luxury >$1.6M) (e4) shows much larger jumps when the product changes, which belongs in the type, not this multiplier. Mid 1.50; high 1.80 for trophy/high-end residential.

items.notes: Above ~1.8x the project is usually a different product type (e.g., luxury hotel vs select-service) and should be modeled as such.

range.method: factor = (projectSize / typicalSize) ^ b, applied to hard cost per SF; clamp the factor to 0.85-1.20. Terner's California regression gives -$0.23/SF per additional unit (e7); at the report's 2018 average of $222/SF, going from 50 to 100 units lowers cost ~$11.5/SF = -5.2%, i.e. b = ln(0.948)/ln(2) = -0.077 -> mid -0.08. GAO/Abt LIHTC data likewise find projects under 37 units cost more than projects over 100 (e9). Low/high (-0.12 / -0.04) by judgment. RSMeans area-modification curves are paywalled and not used.

items.name: Size factor at half the typical size
Size factor at twice the typical size
IBC Type V-A (protected wood frame) — reference
items.notes: Typical garden/walk-up multifamily and many low-rise commercial buildings. A 'V over I' podium sits between V-A and Type I in proportion to the podium share of floor area.

items.name: IBC Type III (A/B — noncombustible exterior walls, wood interior)

range.method: ICC BVD Aug 2025 IIIB/VA and IIIA/VA: R-2 1.102 / 1.139; B 1.079 / 1.119; R-1 1.079 / 1.109 (e5). Mid ~ average.

items.name: IBC Type IV (heavy / mass timber)

range.method: ICC BVD Aug 2025 IV/VA: R-2 1.261, B 1.178, R-1 1.210 (e5); mid 1.21. ICC's single 'IV' column does not separate the 2021-IBC mass-timber types IV-A/B/C; taller IV-A buildings with full encapsulation likely cost more, so high is extended to 1.30 by judgment. No public mass-timber vs concrete cost study was fetched.

items.notes: Verify — mass timber premiums are project-specific and schedule savings are not captured here.

items.name: IBC Type II (A/B — noncombustible steel / light gauge)

range.method: ICC BVD Aug 2025 IIB/VA and IIA/VA: R-2 1.264 / 1.324; B 1.225 / 1.279; R-1 1.213 / 1.260 (e5). Mid ~ average.

items.name: IBC Type I (A/B — fire-resistive concrete / protected steel)

range.method: ICC BVD Aug 2025 IB/VA and IA/VA: R-2 1.383 / 1.444; B 1.327 / 1.376; R-1 1.306 / 1.354 (e5). Terner's California regression finds Type I $65-$71/SF above other types at a $222/SF average (e6), i.e. roughly 1.30-1.35x, consistent with the lower half. Mid 1.37.

items.notes: Typical high-rise. ICC data understate the premium where Type I also brings structured parking or deep foundations.

items.name: Height premium per story above the type's typical story count (same construction type)

range.method: Derived. Most of the height premium arrives through the forced change of construction type (V -> III -> I), which the constructionType factors capture (Type I is +30%-44% over V-A, e5/e6). Within a type, added stories bring more elevator stops, heavier lateral system, taller MEP risers and hoisting, partly offset by spreading roof and foundation over more floor area; ~1% of hard cost per added story (0.5%-2%) by judgment. Do not apply below the typical story count (no discount).

items.notes: Low confidence; apply after the construction-type factor, not instead of it.

items.name: Prevailing wage (Davis-Bacon / state) or union labor premium

range.method: Terner California regression: prevailing-wage projects cost ~$30-$36/SF more (e6), = 13.5%-16% of the $222/SF average. Terner LIHTC study: TDC gap ~10% in San Francisco/San Jose/Los Angeles, 27.5% Central Valley, 36.4% Sacramento; CTCAC allows a 20% increase to cost limits for prevailing wage (e8). Mid 15% (regression); low 10% (high-union metros); high 35% (low-wage open-shop markets).

items.notes: Multiplier on hard cost = 1 + value. The premium is largest where open-shop wages are lowest.
